implementation_notes: TypeScript declares the layer's type with an abstract class: it cannot be instantiated, may combine implemented members (shared state, protected helpers) with abstract members every subclass must implement, and the compiler rejects a subclass that forgets one. Interfaces cover the other half - a pure structural contract with no runtime footprint, implementable by unrelated classes - and the two compose: an abstract base can implement an interface and add shared behavior, so consumers depend on the interface while members extend the base. Remember that abstract exists only at compile time: the emitted JavaScript has ordinary constructors and prototype chains.
pitfalls: abstract is erased at compile time: plain JavaScript callers can instantiate the base or ignore the abstract members, so boundaries still need runtime validation.
protected members become part of every subclass's API, and tightening them later is as breaking as changing public members.
Interfaces erase entirely while abstract classes emit a prototype chain, so using a class for a pure contract adds runtime footprint and single-inheritance coupling.
